Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with a white sail on a calm teal sea at sunset

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

15 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: the sailboat's white sail and red hull Light: the low sun, centre of the picture just above the horizon, shining toward the viewerHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Brush on the orange skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Dab in the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Paint the hill and shorelineFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Dash in the soft gray-green patchesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • small round: Dash the bright glintsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • liner: Line in the mastLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way), and masking tape to mark halves and quarters along its edges.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. On your 14 x 11 in canvas the marks across the top are 3 1/2 in apart and the marks down the side 2 3/4 in apart. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The red hull; 2 The white sails. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 4.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 5.
  • Horizontal strokes, first in step 6.
  • Horizontal dashes, first in step 7.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 11.
  • Liner work, first in step 12. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.
  • Pull-down, first in step 13.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The sunset sky 3 steps

STEP 1 OF 15 · The sunset sky, 1 of 3

Brush on the orange sky

  1. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  2. Paint: Sunset orange.
  3. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  4. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  5. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  6. Watch out: A hard line where two colors meet. Fix: add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

Tip: The light comes from the low sun in the middle of the picture, so every glow is brightest around it. Colors dry a little darker, so test your orange on the edge of the palette first. Paint straight through where the sail and the sun will go; the sail covers it later.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 15 · The sunset sky, 2 of 3

Blend in the coral band

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 3/4 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Rosy coral.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  5. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  6. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  7. Leave what step 1 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: A hard line where two colors meet. Fix: add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

Tip: Work from the top of the coral band down into the wet orange and stop as soon as the paint starts to drag. Leave orange showing low down, near the horizon.

STEP 3 OF 15 · The sunset sky, 3 of 3

Blend in the violet top

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Dusk violet.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  5. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  6. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  7. Leave what steps 1 and 2 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: A hard line where two colors meet. Fix: add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Start at the top edge with violet and soften it down into the coral. Keep the violet to roughly the top fifth of the sky; the glow stays strongest around the sun. The orange around the sun gets a little brighter and warmer as you blend; keep it glowing right around the sun.

The setting sun 1 step

STEP 4 OF 15 · The setting sun, 1 of 1

Dab in the sun

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 3/4 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Pale sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Around a sun, make small circles with the tip of the brush, moving outward from the middle, to build a soft round disc.
  7. It should leave a soft round disc with a slightly bumpy edge.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter passes. On a cloud, smudging with a finger works too.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is a small round disc, about 3/4 inch across, just left of the middle and sitting above the far hill line. Dab it in with two or three light coats, letting the paint set between, so the orange does not show through.

The far hill 1 step

STEP 5 OF 15 · The far hill, 1 of 1

Paint the hill and shoreline

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  4. Paint: Deep indigo.
  5. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  6. Bend every stroke with the shape: follow the slope of the hill, down the left side and along the flat shoreline.
  7. It should leave marks that follow the hill's slope, which is what makes it look like a rounded hill.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The hill rises on the left and slopes gently down to the right, then thins into a flat dark shoreline that runs all the way across to the right edge, behind the boat. Keep the strokes following the slope of the hill.

Stroke: Curved strokes how to do it, not checked yet

Curved strokes

Not checked yet

Motion. Bend every stroke with the shape: down each rib of a pumpkin from the top of the bump, around a balloon.

What it leaves. Marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.

Then. Use the darker mix along the shadow side and the lighter one along the lit side, both following the curve.

The sea 2 steps

STEP 6 OF 15 · The sea, 1 of 2

Lay in the deep teal sea

  1. Let the far hill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Deep teal.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave flat, level bands that read as ground or water stretching away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.

Tip: The sea starts at the shoreline and runs to the bottom edge. Use long, level strokes. Around now the painting looks flat and plain; that is the ugly stage and it is normal.

STEP 7 OF 15 · The sea, 2 of 2

Dash in the soft gray-green patches

  1. Let the sea and the far hill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Gray-green teal.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint, a light touch.
  5. Short, level dashes. Small and close together near the horizon, longer and wider apart lower down.
  6. It should leave short, flat, level marks with gaps of the water color between them.
  7. Leave what step 6 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: The dashes smear into the water. The water underneath is still wet. Fix: paint them over dry water only.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Make the dashes short and close together near the horizon and longer and wider apart toward you. Leave plenty of the deep teal showing between them. A few of these dashes pick up a warm gold flicker from the sunset; that is fine, the glitter path comes next.

The sun's glitter path 2 steps

STEP 8 OF 15 · The sun's glitter path, 1 of 2

Dash the dim gold glints

  1. Let the sea and the far hill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

  3. Paint: Muted gold-brown.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint, a light touch.

The red sailboat 3 steps

STEP 10 OF 15 · The red sailboat, 1 of 3

Paint the red hull

  1. Let the sea and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 1 in tall.
  5. Paint: Boat red.
  6. Mix enough Boat red for this step and step 14; cover it between them.
  7. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  8. Bend every stroke with the shape: follow the curve of the hull from one end to the other.
  9. It should leave marks that follow the hull's curve, which is what makes it look round.

Tip: The hull is a shallow curved bowl, wider at the top, sitting on the sea on the right. Keep each stroke following the curve of its bottom.

  5. Paint: Warm sail white.
  6. Mix enough Warm sail white for this step and step 15; cover it between them.
  7. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  8. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.
  9. It should leave a shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Tip: Make a tall triangle for the wider sail on the left, and a slimmer one on its right, meeting at the mast line. Start at the bottom corner and pull each stroke up toward the tip. Leave the mast line free for the next step.

STEP 12 OF 15 · The red sailboat, 3 of 3

Line in the mast

  1. Let the white sails and the red hull dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 1/2 in wide and 4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Mast dark.
  5. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  6. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull one straight upright line from the hull up to the tip of the sails, and keep the edges steady.
  7. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  8. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Run one straight upright line from the middle of the hull to a little above the sail tip. Keep it vertical and steady; go slowly. The sails' center line is where it goes.

Pull down the soft blue-gray

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat at sunset on a calm sea

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders or text.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 11 x 14 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: about 15% of the width, split between empty sky/sea at both edges

Why: The subject is the boat on the right and the sun and path in the middle; crop is free.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things (the boat is the subject), no textures of hundreds of items, no detail inside big shapes beyond one repeated mark, and 6 parts with no parent (sky, hill, water, hull, sail, mast), within the budget of 8.

Why: Every answer was no.

A calm sunset seascape: the strong sky gradient, the glittering sun path, and one small red sailboat with its reflection. Hard parts are the sky blend (violet to coral to orange) and the reflections. The lesson is about back-to-front layering and horizontal strokes.

Subject: A small red sailboat with a white sail on a calm teal sea at sunset
Focal point: the sailboat's white sail and red hull
Light: the low sun, centre of the picture just above the horizon, shining toward the viewer

What it saw, back to front

  1. Sunset sky
  2. The far hill and shore
  3. The sea
  4. The red hull
  5. The white sails
  6. The mast
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, fits a beginner and a scene made of sky, hill, sea and one object; water reflection rules are in the technique.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It starts with a toned canvas and a block-in stage; the owner picked paint-along for acrylic beginners.

How the paint recipes were worked out16 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order15 steps

Sky first (straight through past the horizon), then sun and hill, sea, glitter path, then the boat, then its reflection last once the boat is dry.

  1. 1. Brush on the orange sky

    Orange base coat for the whole sky, first because it is farthest back.

  2. 2. Blend in the coral band

    Coral band blended in while the orange is still workable.

  3. 3. Blend in the violet top

    Violet top of the sky, lightest-to-darkest blend finish.

  4. 4. Dab in the sun

    The sun sits on the finished sky; one small disc.

  5. 5. Paint the hill and shoreline

    The far hill and shoreline, painted over the finished sky.

  6. 6. Lay in the deep teal sea

    Teal base for all the water, before anything that sits on it.

  7. 7. Dash in the soft gray-green patches

    Lighter gray-green dashes give the ripples over the dry base.

  8. 8. Dash the dim gold glints

    Dim gold under the sun, the base of the glitter path.

  9. 9. Dash the bright glints

    Bright glints on top, covering less than the dim coat.

  10. 10. Paint the red hull

    The red hull sits on the water, painted over the dry sea.

  11. 11. Paint the white sails

    Sails above the hull, in front of the sky.

  12. 12. Line in the mast

    Mast last of the boat; thin line over dry sails.

  13. 13. Pull down the soft blue-gray

    Soft blue-gray base of the reflection, after the boat is dry.

  14. 14. Pull down the red

    Red under the hull, small.

  15. 15. Pull down the white

    White streaks, the last and lightest.

What the reviewer caught5 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check Finish is more saturated than the photo: the sea is a bluer teal, the sky violet stronger. No redo (colors still sunset-orange/violet/teal).
  • Text check: flat Step 1: step pictures 1-5 show a boat-shaped patch of rough fill and a white speck at the sun before their steps (left: outline holes of the sail and sun in the sky/sea parts; a second outline round after the background was not tried)
  • Text check: missing Step 3: sun glow brightening not covered (fixed)
  • Text check: missing Step 7: gold flecks and dark bands appear in the sea pass (fixed)
  • Text check: missing Step 15: mast reflection zigzag line appears (fixed)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Paints measured four colors for the thin mast (mast-2..4 are leaked sea/sail/sunset colors); three go unused. Base mixes 15 against target 10.
  • The finish is more saturated than the photo.
  • Drafted lines rewritten: curved-strokes card (pumpkin/balloon text) on the hill and hull; small-circles card (cloud text) on the sun; liner card (branches text) on the mast; pull-down card (tree, boat or shore) on the reflections.
  • No card for a mast reflection zigzag as its own step; the zigzag card exists but the reflection part has no mast paint.
  • Boat-shaped ghost patch and a white speck at the sun remain in early step pictures.
